title: 5 Reasons Why the Best Microsoft Teams Migrations Start Long Before Deployment
summary: Planning a Microsoft Teams migration? Discover five reasons why organizational readiness, user needs, governance and testing should come before deployment.
body_markdown:
Microsoft Teams migrations can look deceptively straightforward on a project plan. Licenses are assigned, infrastructure is prepared and a rollout date is agreed. Yet the real test begins when employees are expected to change how they communicate, make calls, join meetings and collaborate every day.


Microsoft’s own adoption guidance reflects this reality. Its Teams framework separates adoption into Start, Experiment and Scale phases, with early adopters, governance decisions and user feedback coming before broad deployment. 1


Microsoft also recommends assessing organizational readiness for change as part of the initial adoption phase. 2


That points to a useful distinction – being technically ready for Microsoft Teams is not the same as being organizationally ready for it. A successful Teams transformation depends on both.


So what separates a successful Microsoft Teams migration from one that simply gets deployed? Here are five reasons why the work done before rollout matters.


➊


---


## Teams Migration Is Really an Organizational Change Project


Microsoft Teams has considerable reach. Microsoft report that Teams serves more than 320 million monthly active users across 181 markets and 44 languages. 3


But scale does not make adoption automatic.


Microsoft explicitly describes change as a human process and advises organizations to assess stakeholders, identify early adopters and understand how different groups respond to change before moving ahead. 4


That matters because employees rarely work in identical ways. Frontline staff may depend heavily on reliable voice communications. Hybrid knowledge workers move between meetings, chat and files. Executives may prioritize high-quality meeting experiences while IT teams need manageable endpoints, governance and operational visibility.


Treat everyone as the same persona and a technically successful rollout can still produce an inconsistent employee experience.


➋


---


## Discovery Should Come Before Deployment


The first question should therefore not be “When can we migrate?” It should be “How does this organization actually communicate?”


Discovery can expose dependencies that are easy to miss in an infrastructure-led assessment, such as legacy PBXs, existing unified communications platforms, specialist voice workflows, meeting room requirements, different employee personas and governance considerations.


Microsoft recommends environmental discovery covering existing collaboration infrastructure, networking, endpoints, operations and adoption readiness. It describes discovery as an early step for identifying risks and potential blockers before a Teams rollout. 5


This changes the migration conversation. Instead of designing around technology first, organizations can design around the people who will use it.


➌


---


## Why Personas Matter to Microsoft Teams Adoption


A persona-based strategy aligns technology with how employees actually work. Teams Phone, desk phones, headsets and meeting room systems can then be matched to each group’s communication needs, user experience and operational requirements rather than deployed uniformly.


Microsoft similarly recommends identifying user profiles and business scenarios when planning Teams adoption. 6


The goal is simple – less friction between employees and the way they need to work.

## Pilot the Experience, Not Just the Technology


A proof of concept should test whether Teams works for the organization, not simply whether it works. Real employees can validate call quality, meeting experiences, workflows, governance and new devices before User Acceptance Testing confirms readiness for rollout.


Microsoft similarly recommends piloting Teams with business users, champions and IT professionals before wider adoption. 7


Problems found during a controlled pilot are far easier to manage than after enterprise-wide migration.


➎


---


## Readiness Does Not End at Go-Live


Microsoft Teams readiness is not a box to tick before migration. In fact, Microsoft recommends an ongoing adoption plan after deployment because employees can revert to old ways of working. It also advises organizations to establish a change cycle as Teams and Microsoft 365 gain new functionality. 8


Organizations therefore need to monitor adoption, network and call quality, governance requirements and employee experience after rollout. Optimization becomes part of operating Teams rather than a separate post-migration exercise.

###


Organizational readiness is the process of assessing whether people, processes, governance, infrastructure and support models are prepared for Microsoft Teams. It complements technical readiness by considering how employees actually work and respond to change.


###


A pilot allows organizations to test business scenarios with real employees before scaling deployment. Microsoft recommends experimentation with early adopters so organizations can gather feedback and make governance and lifecycle decisions before broad rollout. 9


###


A comprehensive assessment should consider existing collaboration and voice infrastructure, networking, endpoints, operational processes, employee personas, governance and adoption readiness. Microsoft includes these areas in its own environmental discovery guidance. 10
